title: Balanitis in a child
presentation: A boy with a red, sore foreskin and glans, possibly with discharge. Age to be added.

groups.name: Infective
items: Rarely sexually transmitted or linked to abuse, so consider safeguarding

tables.title: Physiological vs pathological phimosis
rows: Common in young boys; usually separates by teenage years (verify)

investigations.test: Examination of foreskin, glans, urethral meatus, testes
Swab if discharge or no response

management: Saline or warm bathing, gentle hygiene without forced retraction.
Avoid soaps and irritants, keep the area dry.
Topical antimicrobial only if indicated (check BNFc).
Safety-netting: return if swelling, pain passing urine, fever, or no improvement in a few days.
Refer to paediatric surgery or urology for recurrent episodes, scarring or pathological phimosis.
redFlags: Fever, systemic upset or urinary retention
Suspicion of non-accidental injury or abuse
pearls: Do not forcibly retract the foreskin.
Explain hygiene to the parent and child kindly and without blame.
lookUp: NICE CKS balanitis and when to refer
Age at which foreskin normally retracts

selfTest.q: What urgent complication must you exclude?
selfTest.a: Paraphimosis; also torsion if testicular pain.

selfTest.q: Why consider glucose in recurrent balanitis?
selfTest.a: It may be the first sign of diabetes.
